scenes.tts: Two plots hold the same four species. Each plot has one hundred individuals. In plot A, every species has twenty-five. In plot B, the counts are forty, forty, ten and ten. Is one plot more diverse? The answer depends on what you decide to count.
scenes.caption: Two plots hold the same four species. Each plot has 100 individuals. In plot A, every species has 25. In plot B, the counts are 40, 40, 10 and 10. Is one plot more diverse? The answer depends on what you decide to count.
scenes.visual: Two 10 by 10 dot plots, four marker shapes; counts under each; a question mark between them.
scenes.narration: Two plots hold the same four species. Each plot has 100 individuals. In plot A, every species has 25. In plot B, the counts are 40, 40, 10 and 10. Is one plot more diverse? The answer depends on what you decide to count.

scenes.tts: Start with richness. Richness is the number of species present. Both plots have four, so richness is tied. But richness ignores abundance. It cannot see that plot B has two common species and two rare ones. To see that, use relative abundance. That is the share of all individuals that belong to each species. In plot A, every share is point two five.

In plot A, every share is 0.25.
scenes.visual: Plots shrink; species marks counted, S = 4 and a tie sign; count bars grow; labels change to shares.
scenes.narration: Start with richness. Richness is the number of species present. Both plots have four, so richness is tied. But richness ignores abundance. It cannot see that plot B has two common species and two rare ones. To see that, use relative abundance. That is the share of all individuals that belong to each species. In plot A, every share is 0.25.

scenes.tts: Now try Simpson concentration. Pull two individuals at random, putting the first back before the second. Simpson concentration, called lambda, is the chance that both belong to the same species. In plot A, lambda is point two five. In plot B, it is point three four. Lambda runs the opposite way from the other measures. It rises as one species dominates.
scenes.caption: Now try Simpson concentration. Pull two individuals at random, putting the first back before the second. It rises as one species dominates.
scenes.visual: Unit square with one square per species of side p; area of the squares is lambda.

scenes.tts: Nats and probabilities are hard to compare. So convert each measure to an effective number of species. That is the number of equally common species that would give the same value. For plot A, the answer is four point zero zero by every measure. For plot B, Shannon entropy gives three point three zero species. Inverse Simpson gives two point nine four.
scenes.caption: Nats and probabilities are hard to compare. So convert each measure to an effective number of species. That is the number of equally common species that would give the same value. For plot A, the answer is 4.00 by every measure. For plot B, Shannon entropy gives 3.30 species. Inverse Simpson gives 2.94.
scenes.visual: H and lambda values turn into rows of equal blocks: 4, 4.00, 4.00 for A; 4, 3.30, 2.94 for B.
scenes.narration: Nats and probabilities are hard to compare. So convert each measure to an effective number of species. That is the number of equally common species that would give the same value. For plot A, the answer is 4.00 by every measure. For plot B, Shannon entropy gives 3.30 species. Inverse Simpson gives 2.94.

scenes.tts: Notice the pattern in plot B. Order zero gives four species. The next order gives three point three. The one after gives two point nine four. Higher orders give more weight to common species. So plot B's two rare species count for less as the order rises. Evenness is inverse Simpson divided by richness. It is one for plot A and zero point seven three five for plot B.
scenes.caption: Notice the pattern in plot B. Order 0 gives 4 species. The next order gives 3.3. The one after gives 2.94. Higher orders give more weight to common species. So plot B's two rare species count for less as the order rises. Evenness is inverse Simpson divided by richness. It is 1 for plot A and 0.735 for plot B.
scenes.visual: The three rows are stepped through; B's rare dots dim; evenness values appear.
scenes.narration: Notice the pattern in plot B. Order 0 gives 4 species. The next order gives 3.3. The one after gives 2.94. Higher orders give more weight to common species. So plot B's two rare species count for less as the order rises. Evenness is inverse Simpson divided by richness. It is 1 for plot A and 0.735 for plot B.

scenes.tts: Now swap the labels on plot B's species. Every number stays the same. No index sees which species are present. Two plots with identical indices can share no species at all. Each measure misses something. Richness ignores abundance. Higher orders discount rare species. So always name the measure you used, and say what it misses.
